blocks.text: Study designs are classified by (1) how subjects are identified — by exposure vs. by outcome — and (2) time course: prospective (forward from exposure to outcome), retrospective (backward from outcome to exposure), or cross-sectional (both measured together, a 'snapshot'). Descriptive studies (case reports/series, cross-sectional/prevalence studies, census) describe a group without testing a causal hypothesis or comparing groups; analytical studies (case-control, cohort) compare two groups to measure association; experimental studies are prospective designs where exposure is deliberately assigned (RCTs), unlike cohort studies where exposure occurs naturally.

Case-control studies are retrospective: both exposure and disease have already occurred at the time subjects are recruited. They are easy to carry out, less time-consuming, less expensive, and most useful for diseases where exposure is common but the disease occurs in only a small proportion of those exposed (rare diseases) — with no attrition problems since there is no follow-up.

In cohort studies, relative risk (**RR**) can be calculated as the ratio of disease (outcome) in the exposed to disease in the non-exposed; the odds ratio can also be calculated from cohort studies. Case-control studies, by contrast, cannot directly measure incidence (no longitudinal observation), so a cross-product ratio called the odds ratio is used instead of **RR**.

blocks.subtopic: Attributable risk (AR) — sign properties
blocks.note: Not covered in books/15-1-statistics.pdf — tested via the question bank: attributable risk (AR) is an absolute risk *difference* and **CAN** be negative when risk in the exposed is lower than in the unexposed, unlike relative risk (a *ratio*), which can never be negative.

blocks.text: Cross-sectional studies (also called prevalence studies) describe attributes of a study group at a single point in time — a 'snapshot'. They can only estimate prevalence; incidence rates require a cohort study that follows a population forward over time.

A cross-sectional (prevalence) study is the design of choice for measuring the point prevalence of a clinical problem within a group — a single-point-in-time 'snapshot', as opposed to period or lifetime prevalence measured differently.
Prospective longitudinal (cohort) studies are needed to study the natural course of illness, study risk factors, and find out incidence rates — though they are costly and time-consuming.

Case-control advantages: easy to carry out, less time-consuming, less expensive, suitable for investigating rare diseases, subjects are not exposed to any new risks, several different aetiological factors for a single disease can be studied, and there are no attrition problems. Disadvantages: highly prone to selection and recall bias, control-group selection may be difficult, incidence cannot be measured (so only odds ratio, not relative risk), it cannot prove causality, and temporality is difficult to determine retrospectively.

blocks.subtopic: Survival analysis — suited study designs
blocks.note: Not covered in books/15-1-statistics.pdf — tested via the question bank: cohort studies (and, to a lesser extent, parallel RCTs) are the design suited to survival analysis, since only follow-up data from a defined starting point to a defined event allow this; cross-over trials and cross-sectional surveys are unsuited.

blocks.text: Though generally cohort studies are prospective, it is possible to do a retrospective cohort study by identifying a cohort using existing records and then tracing them forward to see if they developed a disease of interest — e.g. identifying military recruits from 1940 who were physically disfigured (exposure), then tracing forward to 1998 to observe development of **PTSD**, compared to recruits from the same year who were not disfigured. This remains a cohort design even though data collection happens after the fact.

Cohort study disadvantages: difficult to carry out as it is more time/resource-consuming, and it is not suitable for investigating rare diseases (thousands of exposed persons must be observed). Advantages: less prone to selection and recall bias, incidence (and so relative risk) can be measured, causal association can be more strongly supported than with case-control design, temporality is established easily, dose-response relationships can be calculated, and the natural course of exposure-to-disease can be studied.

A cross-sectional design is the correct choice for evaluating a screening tool against a gold-standard reference, since a cross-sectional study measures exposure and outcome — here, the tool's result and the true diagnosis — together, at a single point in time, in the same subjects.

A cross-sectional study is also the correct design to establish the proportion of people with a comorbid condition within an existing population (e.g. mental illness among those who are alcohol-dependent) — a prevalence question answered with a single-point-in-time snapshot of that population.

blocks.text: Case-control studies gain power by increasing the control:case ratio up to 4:1; beyond that ratio, power does not increase further. If disease prevalence is <==5%== (the rare-disease assumption), the odds ratio approximates relative risk.

Overzealous matching of cases/controls can make recruitment difficult, can shrink the risk difference between groups, and may inadvertently match on a causal factor itself; because the odds ratio ranges 0 to infinity (no negative values), log transformation is needed to derive its confidence interval.
A nested case-control study draws both cases and controls from within an existing cohort rather than studying the whole cohort — cheaper, with similar precision.

Ecological studies use group/population-level exposure data, not individual-level — there is an assumption that all members of a population are equally exposed and carry the same risk, disregarding within-group differences. E.g. concluding that low religious attachment causes suicide from a country-level correlation tells nothing about whether the individuals who died by suicide were themselves religious.
Ecological fallacy is drawing subject-level conclusions based on group-level observations made in an ecological study.
Case reports and case series are the simplest forms of descriptive studies — they describe the characteristics of a group of subjects with no testing of a causal hypothesis and no comparison group.

blocks.subtopic: Denominator specification when comparing incidence rates across time periods
blocks.note: Not covered in books/15-1-statistics.pdf — tested via the question bank: comparing incidence rates across time periods requires an appropriately specified denominator (e.g. the mid-period population) — omitting this invalidates the comparison, even in a purely retrospective descriptive survey needing no randomisation or control group.

blocks.text: Pragmatic RCTs select clinically relevant alternative interventions, include a diverse population from heterogeneous practice settings, minimise exclusion criteria, and collect data on a broad range of health outcomes. They do not tell how well a drug works under optimal conditions (efficacy) — they inform how effective the intervention is in the real world, giving **HIGHER** external validity/generalisability than explanatory (efficacy) trials, not lower.

RCTs differ from natural clinical practice in numerous, simultaneous ways: recruitment from specialist centres, exclusion of patients with co-morbid medical or psychiatric disorders, careful selection to generate homogeneous diagnostic groups, random (non-negotiated) treatment allocation, detailed informed consent, placebo comparison, more frequent follow-up than usual care, detailed side-effect checklists, a typically short (4-6 week) assessment endpoint, symptom-scale outcomes, and blinding of patient and clinician.

blocks.subtopic: Surrogate endpoint (vs secondary outcome)
blocks.note: Not covered in books/15-1-statistics.pdf — tested via the question bank: a surrogate endpoint is a proxy measure substituted for the outcome of real clinical interest (e.g. using duration of untreated psychosis, DUP, as a stand-in for psychosis-related disability) — distinct from a secondary outcome measure, which tests a different, additional hypothesis.

blocks.text: Stopping a trial early after an interim analysis shows a large apparent benefit tends to **OVERESTIMATE** the true treatment effect — this is a small-numbers/chance artefact, not evidence the intervention truly works even better than a completed trial would show.

blocks.subtopic: Hierarchy of evidence for therapy questions
blocks.note: Not covered in books/15-1-statistics.pdf — the Oxford Centre for EBM-style hierarchy (secondary research/systematic reviews > single RCT > uncontrolled/non-experimental designs) is covered properly under this app's evidence-based-medicine topic guide, not here.

blocks.text: A survey's response/completion rate is **NOT** the same statistic as a study's statistical power — a vignette quoting ==74%==/==60%==/==88%== response rates across groups is testing whether you know power cannot be inferred from response rate alone.

When a results figure collapses 'agree' and 'strongly agree' into a single headline percentage (e.g. ==67%== vs ==24%==), that combined figure is **NOT** the same as the proportion who answered 'strongly agree' alone — read the individual bar, not the reported headline comparison.
Parallel-design RCT: both control and intervention groups proceed in parallel, not serially — the most common form of RCT.

Crossover-design RCT: an interchange of study and control groups after a washout period, so all subjects receive both placebo and treatment, only in a different order. This is an economical design, needing fewer subjects — but it cannot be used for diseases that are cured by the medication under study (no reversible baseline to cross back to).

Factorial-design RCT: two or more interventions are evaluated both separately and in combination against a control — e.g. a 2x2 factorial design allocates participants to one of four combinations (2 treatments, 2 levels), testing both each drug's independent effect and their combined effect.

Worked factorial-RCT example (Heinala et al. 2001, J Clin Psychopharmacol): naltrexone vs no naltrexone, crossed with cognitive coping-skills therapy (**CCT**) vs no **CCT**, for alcohol dependence — the four combinations were naltrexone+**CCT**, naltrexone only, **CCT** only, and placebo/neither.

blocks.subtopic: Non-randomised controlled trial (named term)
blocks.note: Not covered in books/15-1-statistics.pdf — tested via the question bank: a non-randomised controlled trial has a genuine control arm, but allocation is not random (e.g. alternating consecutive patients between two treatments) — distinct from a pragmatic RCT, which remains randomised.

blocks.subtopic: Quasi-experimental study (named term)
blocks.note: Not covered in books/15-1-statistics.pdf — tested via the question bank: a quasi-experimental study shares the structure of a true experiment but lacks random assignment of participants to intervention groups (e.g. clinicians choosing freely between two formulations based on clinical judgement).

blocks.text: Uncontrolled trials observe only one group for the effects of an intervention — there is no control group, and inference is instead made using a historical control (the treated group's own status before intervention). A before-and-after trial extends this to assess outcome before and after an intervention in one group — the observed change may in fact be attributable to a factor other than the intervention itself, making this design inherently weak, and there is no randomisation.

blocks.subtopic: Interrupted time series / controlled before-and-after study (named terms)
blocks.note: Not covered in books/15-1-statistics.pdf — tested via the question bank: an interrupted time series takes repeated measurements before and after the 'interruption'; a controlled before-and-after study adds a genuine second group also measured before and after.

blocks.text: Block randomisation occurs in sets of specified size (e.g. blocks of 6) to ensure equal number distribution between arms — the larger the block size, the harder it is to predict the next allocation.

Stratified randomisation stratifies baseline characteristics that may affect the final outcome so that equal distribution across groups is enforced. The gain in precision through stratification is minimal for large studies, and stratification does not eliminate the need for adjustment for baseline differences between groups if they are still found.

Cluster randomisation randomises at the level of a centre or catchment-zone, not the individual patient — everyone within an allocated cluster receives the same arm. Patients within a cluster tend to respond more similarly to one another, so they cannot be assumed to act as independent units; this loss of independence causes a loss of statistical power compared with individual-patient randomisation. Power calculations therefore use effective sample size (**ESS**), derived from a measure of within-cluster similarity called the intracluster correlation.

Minimisation is useful when a stratified randomisation is wanted but the trial is too small for it, or when a cluster randomisation leaves too few units — the next participant's allocation depends on the characteristics of those already allocated, aiming to balance prognostic factors between groups. It is considered inferior to true randomisation because allocation becomes somewhat predictable/manually 'controlled' — in fact, only the first allocation is truly random.

Quasi-randomisation (e.g. odd/even last digit of date of birth, day of the week seen) 'randomises' using non-reproducible methods that cannot ensure equal distribution of prognostic variables — these must be avoided.

Odd/even birth-date or day-of-the-week 'randomisation' is quasi-randomisation, not true randomisation — it is not reproducible and cannot guarantee equal distribution of prognostic variables, even though allocation still technically occurs before the patient is examined.

blocks.subtopic: Sequential RCT (named design)
blocks.note: Not covered in books/15-1-statistics.pdf — tested via the question bank: participants are recruited into each group until investigators can clearly determine a difference (or lack of difference) between groups — sample size is not fixed a priori, analysis is done at intervals, and the trial is stopped by a pre-specified stopping rule, which can lower overall trial cost.

blocks.text: Uses of randomisation: it permits use of probability theory in making inferences, eliminates the effects of bias, facilitates blinding, and distributes baseline characteristics in an unpredictable fashion across groups (balancing, but not guaranteeing freedom from, confounders). It can be performed at a cluster as well as an individual level, and it improves generalisability — pragmatic RCTs remain randomised yet highly generalisable.

Randomisation improves generalisability, but it does not ensure results will always be precise — precision depends on sample size. Having a large sample size does not mean randomisation is unnecessary.

A large sample size chiefly buys representativeness — it is not a substitute for randomisation, and randomisation itself does not automatically guarantee precision of estimates; these are three separate statistical properties frequently bundled together as distractors in the same question.

bullets.text: Case-control: retrospective, cheap, fast, best for rare diseases or diseases with long latency; can study several aetiological factors for one disease at once. Cohort: prospective (usually), can measure incidence/RR, better temporality, but time/resource-consuming and prone to attrition.
Cross-sectional (prevalence) studies are a single-point-in-time snapshot — they can only estimate prevalence, never incidence (which needs a cohort study).

A retrospective cohort study still counts as a cohort design even when exposure groups are defined from historical records and outcome is determined by tracing forward (e.g. 1940 military recruits traced to 1998 for PTSD).
Case-control power gains from raising the control:case ratio plateau beyond 4:1. If disease prevalence is <5% (rare-disease assumption), the odds ratio approximates relative risk.

Because the odds ratio ranges 0 to infinity (no negative values), log transformation is needed to derive its confidence interval. Overzealous case/control matching can shrink the risk difference and may inadvertently match on a causal factor itself.
A nested case-control study draws both cases and controls from within an existing cohort rather than the whole cohort — cheaper, similar precision.
Ecological studies use group-level exposure data, assuming all members of a population are equally exposed — drawing individual-level conclusions from this is the ecological fallacy.

Pragmatic RCTs select clinically relevant comparators, a diverse population from heterogeneous settings, minimise exclusions, and report real-world effectiveness — giving **HIGHER** external validity than explanatory (efficacy) trials, not lower.

RCTs differ from real clinical practice in many simultaneous ways: specialist-centre recruitment, comorbidity exclusion, homogeneous diagnostic groups, random allocation, detailed consent, placebo comparison, closer monitoring, short (4-6wk) assessment endpoints, symptom-scale outcomes, and blinding.

Crossover RCTs need fewer subjects (each patient is their own control) but cannot be used where the intervention cures the disease. Factorial RCTs (e.g. 2x2) test each intervention's independent effect plus their combination, against a control.

Cluster randomisation allocates whole centres/catchment-zones, not individuals — within-cluster responses correlate, causing a loss of statistical power versus individual randomisation, so power calculations use effective sample size (ESS) via the intracluster correlation.

Minimisation balances prognostic factors when a trial is too small for stratified randomisation or a cluster randomisation leaves too few units — inferior to true randomisation since only the first allocation is truly random.

Randomisation eliminates bias, facilitates blinding, and distributes baseline characteristics unpredictably (balancing, not guaranteeing freedom from, confounders) — it improves generalisability but does not by itself ensure precision, which depends on sample size.
Efficacy = how well a drug works under optimal conditions; effectiveness = how well it works under usual practice; efficiency = whether resources are used to maximise value for money.

blocks.text: Allocation concealment means keeping the random sequence — and so the outcome of the **NEXT** allocation — secret from the investigator, clinician, and patient until assignment is completed, typically via a centralised/remote randomisation service or Serially Numbered, Opaque, Sealed Envelopes (**SNOSE**). This is distinct from blinding, which keeps the allocation secret **AFTER** assignment, through to final outcome measurement.

Allocation concealment (keeping the **NEXT** allocation unpredictable, usually via an independent third party) is a distinct safeguard from blinding (masking the arm **AFTER** allocation) — don't conflate the two when a vignette mentions a third party administering the randomisation sequence.

Blinding levels: open-label (all parties aware of treatment), single-blind (the patient, usually, is unaware of their treatment assignment), double-blind (both patient and investigator are unaware — the most common form), triple-blind (patient, investigator(s), and the assessor who adjudicates outcomes are all unaware). Unblinding is the planned or unintended disclosure of a participant's allocation.

Double-blind = Participant + Investigator (outcome assessor)

blocks.text: Blinding exists because an unblinded clinician may over-react to side effects in the active-treatment group and downplay them in the placebo group; an unblinded patient may report less improvement on placebo or overrate improvement on active treatment; and an unblinded assessor may overrate positive outcomes and underrate ill-effects in the active group. This is chiefly a safeguard against measurement/observer bias, not selection bias.

Sound randomisation requires a reproducible order of assignment, documented methods, concealed assignments, and future assignments that are not predictable from past ones — concealment of allocation specifically refers to whether the **OUTCOME** of randomisation can be predicted in advance.

bullets.text: Allocation concealment keeps the **NEXT** allocation's outcome unpredictable (via a centralised service or SNOSE) — distinct from blinding, which conceals the arm **AFTER** allocation through to outcome measurement.
Blinding chiefly guards against measurement/observer bias (clinician/patient/assessor all rating or reporting differently if unblinded) — **NOT** selection bias.
Sound randomisation needs a reproducible, documented, concealed sequence where future assignments cannot be predicted from past ones.

blocks.text: Intention-to-treat (**ITT**) analysis counts every participant in the group to which they were originally randomised — regardless of adherence, discontinuation, or even crossing over to the other arm — reporting the outcome out of **ALL** those originally randomised, not just those who completed follow-up. This gives a conservative, generalisable/pragmatic estimate and is the preferred default way to report most **RCT** results, since the rationale is to estimate the broader effect of *allocating* an intervention, not the narrower effect in a subgroup who strictly adhere to it.

Per-protocol (**PP**, or 'on-treatment') analysis includes only participants who adequately complied with the trial protocol — the intentional antithesis of **ITT**. It is often carried out in biological/explanatory **RCTs** and as a secondary analysis within effectiveness trials.

Per-protocol analysis is not simply 'a stricter **ITT**' — it deliberately answers a different question (biological efficacy in fully compliant patients) and is the intentional antithesis of intention-to-treat, which answers the real-world effectiveness question.

blocks.text: Advantages of ITT: retains balance in prognostic factors arising from the original random allocation, gives an unbiased estimate of treatment effect, and admits non-compliance/protocol deviations, reflecting a real clinical situation. Limitations: the estimate is generally conservative due to dilution from non-compliance, it favours equality of treatments in equivalence trials, and it is difficult to interpret if a large proportion of participants cross over to the opposite arm. An ideal ITT analysis requires full compliance, no missing responses, and follow-up on all participants.

Worst-case-scenario imputation assumes that all those lost to follow-up did not improve on the trial intervention — the data of these 'treatment failure' subjects are used as a proxy. This extreme assumption is usually carried out as part of a sensitivity analysis.

Last observation carried forward (**LOCF**) is only useful for longitudinal observations using continuous scales — e.g. in a 6-month fluoxetine trial for depression, the 3rd-month **HAMD**/**MADRS** score can be carried forward to the 4th, 5th, and 6th months. Many psychiatric diseases have a natural remitting course that **LOCF** does not allow for — it is 'too good' for controls and 'too stringent' for the patient group.
Mean imputation replaces a drop-out's missing value with the mean of their own treatment group.

blocks.text: Treatment-received (**TR**) analysis groups participants by the treatment they actually received, not their original allocation — this compromises the benefit of random assignment, since one group's data becomes contaminated by subjects who moved to the other arm. **ITT** must remain the norm unless there is overwhelming justification for a different analysis policy.

blocks.note: Not covered in books/15-1-statistics.pdf — tested via the question bank: if a positive trial result (favouring active treatment) still holds even after worst-case-scenario imputation is applied to missing data, this strengthens confidence that the result is not an artefact of drop-outs.

bullets.text: ITT counts every participant in their originally-randomised group regardless of adherence/crossover — conservative, generalisable, the preferred default for reporting RCT results.
Per-protocol (PP/'on-treatment') analysis is the intentional antithesis of ITT — only fully-compliant participants, answering a biological-efficacy question rather than real-world effectiveness.

ITT advantages: unbiased estimate, retains randomisation's prognostic balance, reflects real-world non-compliance. Limitations: conservative due to dilution, favours equality in equivalence trials, hard to interpret with heavy crossover.

LOCF only suits longitudinal continuous-scale data (e.g. carrying a 3rd-month HAMD/MADRS score forward) — it's 'too good' for controls and 'too stringent' for patients in conditions with a natural remitting course.
Treatment-received (TR) analysis groups by actual treatment taken, not allocation — this compromises randomisation's benefit via contamination between groups.

blocks.text: In an N-of-1 trial, a single participant is administered placebo and active intervention (or two different interventions) in tandem, under double-blind conditions, with allocation in each cycle randomly determined (preferably by a third party) and a pharmacist delivering both in identical form. This optimises a treatment schedule for that one individual, but the results cannot be generalised to other patients.

blocks.title: When is an N-of-1 trial indicated or feasible?
rows: The clinician is uncertain a not-yet-started treatment will work; the patient has started a medication but neither is confident of benefit; neither is confident of the optimal dose; symptoms are suspected — but not certain — to be medication adverse effects; the patient insists on a treatment the clinician believes useless/harmful and a negative N-of-1 result might persuade them

Patient is eager to collaborate; the treatment has rapid onset/termination of action and the underlying condition isn't modified by treatment (only symptom control needed); an optimal treatment duration is feasible; patient-important targets are measurable; stopping criteria are identifiable; a pharmacist can help with blinding; strategies exist for gathering/interpreting the outcome

blocks.text: How an N-of-1 trial is conducted: both patient and doctor remain blind; the pharmacist delivers control and active drug in identical form; allocation in each cycle is randomly determined, preferably by a third party. The outcome is measured regularly, and patient and doctor agree in advance when to stop — often after a strong pattern has emerged, sometimes over many treatment cycles. The data is then analysed to see which intervention fared better.

bullets.text: N-of-1 trial: one participant receives placebo and active intervention in tandem, double-blind, allocation randomised by a third party each cycle — optimises that individual's regimen but results are **NOT** generalisable to other patients.

Feasible only when the treatment has rapid onset/termination of action, the underlying condition isn't modified by treatment (symptom control only), and both patient-important outcomes and stopping criteria can be clearly defined.

blocks.text: A confounder must (1) be related to the exposure, (2) be related to the outcome (in terms of prognosis/susceptibility), (3) not lie on the causal pathway between exposure and outcome, and (4) be differently distributed between the groups being compared. Confounders cannot be eliminated — only controlled for. Design-stage methods: restriction, matching, randomisation. Analysis-stage methods: stratification, multivariate/regression adjustment.

Multivariate/regression adjustment is the one confounder-control method applied purely at the analysis stage, producing adjusted (vs crude) rates — restriction, matching, and randomisation must all be built into the study design beforehand. Stratification is also an analysis-stage method: it tabulates results separately across levels/categories of the confounder.

blocks.subtopic: Temporal association as the one Hill criterion case-control cannot establish
blocks.note: Not covered in books/15-1-statistics.pdf — tested via the question bank: temporal association between cause and outcome is the one Hill criterion that a retrospective case-control design cannot itself establish, which is why cohort (or experimental) designs are considered stronger for demonstrating this aspect of causality.

blocks.text: A confounder can only distort an association if it is unevenly distributed between exposed and unexposed groups — this is precisely why randomisation helps control confounding (it makes the two groups more likely to be similar in confounder distribution), even though randomisation does not itself eliminate confounders.

blocks.subtopic: Distinguishing a confounder from an effect modifier via crude vs Mantel-Haenszel-adjusted RR
blocks.note: Not covered in books/15-1-statistics.pdf's confounding/causality section as this specific diagnostic test — tested via the question bank: compare the crude (unstratified) relative risk against the Mantel-Haenszel-adjusted (stratified) relative risk — if crude approximately equals adjusted, the factor is not a confounder; if the RR differs materially between strata, the factor is an effect modifier. A factor can be both.

blocks.subtopic: Mantel-Haenszel as the standard stratified-OR technique in a confounding context
blocks.note: Not covered in books/15-1-statistics.pdf's confounding/causality section this way (the book does name Mantel-Haenszel, but as a fixed-effects meta-analysis method under Secondary Research — see that section) — tested via the question bank as the standard technique for stratified analysis of odds ratios in the presence of confounding.

blocks.subtopic: Matching's practical size limits (small vs large studies)
blocks.note: Not covered in books/15-1-statistics.pdf — tested via the question bank: matching on shared factors is realistic mainly for smaller studies (e.g. a case-control study of ~30 per group) — it is not practical for large cohort studies, RCTs, ecological studies, or cross-sectional surveys.

blocks.text: Bradford Hill's criteria for causality (A causes B): (1) temporal association — A must precede B; (2) dose-response ('biological gradient') — higher/lower doses of A track with higher/lower B; (3) specificity — A precedes B specifically, not C or D; (4) consistency — if A present, B present, and vice versa; (5) plausible biological association; (6) strength of association; (7) absence of reverse causality (B must not be causing A). 'Sensitivity' is **NOT** one of Hill's criteria.

Absence of a dose-response relationship does **NOT** disprove causality: a genuine threshold effect, doses tested outside the effective 'window', an unmeasured confounder, or chance can all mask a truly causal dose-response relationship.

Stratification is the analysis method that can evaluate **BOTH** confounders (by comparing crude vs stratum-adjusted estimates) and effect modifiers (by checking whether the strength of association varies materially across strata) within the same analysis.

blocks.subtopic: Worked crude-vs-adjusted-vs-stratum RR example (bullying and adult depression)
blocks.note: Not covered in books/15-1-statistics.pdf — tested via the question bank: crude RR = 5.0 for bullying and adult depression; strata RRs of 7.0/3.0/1.5 by parental socioeconomic class differ materially from each other, while the Mantel-Haenszel-adjusted RR (3.0) is close to the crude RR — the correct conclusion is that risk is modified by socioeconomic status (an effect modifier), and the reportable headline figure is the adjusted RR (3), not an average or sum across strata.

blocks.text: Restriction as a confounder-control method means avoiding inclusion of the group carrying the significant confounding influence — e.g. not including any older people in a study of antipsychotics and hip fracture, since age itself increases fracture risk irrespective of antipsychotic exposure. This controls confounding but limits sample size.

Using healthy relatives as case-control study controls is a double-edged design choice: it reduces confounding from genuinely family-shared factors, but risks 'overmatching' — losing the ability to demonstrate a true causal association — if the risk factor itself is genetic or otherwise familial.

items.text: Regression/multivariate adjustment is the **ONLY** confounder-control method from the standard list that can be applied at the analysis stage, after data collection — restriction, randomisation, stratification, and matching must all be designed into the study beforehand.

Randomisation does not eliminate confounders — it only ensures they are distributed evenly enough between groups that they cannot distort the comparison. A confounder only distorts results if it is **UNEVENLY** distributed.

When strata differ from one another (an effect modifier is present), the reportable headline result is the Mantel-Haenszel-**ADJUSTED** rate — never a simple average or sum of the individual stratum-specific rates.

'Sensitivity' is a deliberate distractor among Hill's causality criteria — it is explicitly **NOT** one of them; the tested list is temporality, dose-response, specificity, consistency, and biological plausibility.

blocks.text: Koch's postulates (for infectious-disease causality specifically): the agent must be present in every case (consistency); absent in other diseases (specificity); reproduce the disease experimentally; and be recoverable from the experimental disease. Not generalisable to non-infectious illness — Susser's criteria (grouped into 5 categories, 3 considered essential) are the broader alternative.

Rothman's sufficient-component model treats a 'cause' as usually a minimal set of conditions (a sufficient cause/'causal pie') rather than one factor; each component is a component cause, and one that must appear in every sufficient cause is a necessary cause (e.g. H. pylori for gastric ulcer — necessary but not sufficient alone). MacMahon & Pugh's 'web of causation' (1960) describes the mutual, direct/indirect interactions among risk factors; Murray & Lopez extended this into a hierarchical model separating proximal (mechanistic) from distal (empirical) risk factors.

A positive study result can be explained by: (1) selection bias between groups; (2) measurement bias; (3) confounding causing an indirect association; (4) chance (type 1 error); (5) a genuine causal association.

bullets.text: A confounder must relate to both exposure and outcome, not lie on the causal pathway, and be unevenly distributed between groups. Design-stage control: restriction, matching, randomisation. Analysis-stage control: stratification, multivariate/regression adjustment.
Randomisation helps control confounding by making groups more likely to have similar confounder distributions — it does not itself eliminate confounders.
Restriction avoids including the group carrying the confounding influence (e.g. excluding older patients from an antipsychotic/hip-fracture study) — controls confounding but shrinks the sample.

Bradford Hill's 7 criteria: temporal association, dose-response, specificity, consistency, biological plausibility, strength of association, absence of reverse causality. 'Sensitivity' is **NOT** one of them.
Stratification is the one method that evaluates both confounders (crude vs adjusted comparison) and effect modifiers (does association strength vary by stratum) in the same analysis.

blocks.text: Internal validity = how close a study's result is to the truth (threatened by bias); external validity/generalisability = how applicable the result is to the clinician's own population. Bias is a systematic, predictable error from poor design/collection/analysis — unlike random error it does **NOT** shrink with repetition and cannot be fixed at the analysis stage.

Selection bias occurs when the groups selected for a study differ in important factors other than the study variables themselves — the study population does not represent the target population. It can arise from uneven diagnostic procedures, and is minimised by adequate randomisation.

Response bias exists when people who respond to an invitation to participate differ systematically from those who do not — the 'healthy volunteer' effect, where responders are often healthier than the general population. This is particularly relevant when evaluating screening tests.

blocks.subtopic: Comparing responder vs non-responder baseline characteristics at low response rates
blocks.note: Not covered in books/15-1-statistics.pdf's bias section this way (a similar 'test the differences' technique is described for missing/drop-out data under Intention-to-Treat Analysis, not framed here as a response-bias check) — tested via the question bank: when response rates are low, comparing the known baseline characteristics of responders vs non-responders can help judge whether non-response bias is likely.

blocks.subtopic: Pygmalion effect (experimenter expectancy effect)
blocks.note: Not covered in books/15-1-statistics.pdf — tested via the question bank: mere awareness of the study hypothesis can unconsciously bias a researcher's behaviour toward participants in a way that helps produce the expected outcome.

blocks.subtopic: Cointervention (performance) bias — named term
blocks.note: Not covered in books/15-1-statistics.pdf by this name — tested via the question bank: cointervention bias occurs when a clinician gives extra care/attention to one arm but not the other, distinct from the observer/measurement biases the book does name; reduced by double-blinding clinicians.

blocks.subtopic: "Confounding bias" as a named bias category
blocks.note: Not covered in books/15-1-statistics.pdf as a bias subtype — the book treats confounding as a distinct validity threat from bias (see the Causality & Confounding section of this guide), not one of its own named selection/measurement/analysis bias subtypes.

blocks.text: The Hawthorne effect refers to observed respondents minimising their perceived deviation from the norm — occurring especially in cross-sectional surveys that use questionnaires.
Recall bias (a type of measurement bias) occurs when subjects recall risk factors differently depending on their disease status — case-control studies are particularly vulnerable to this.

blocks.subtopic: Rumination bias / exposure-suspicion bias — named subtypes of recall bias
blocks.note: Not covered in books/15-1-statistics.pdf by these specific names — the book names recall bias generally (see above) but not these two named subtypes.

blocks.text: Analysis bias occurs when participants change group (contamination bias) or are lost to follow-up (attrition bias) during a study — this is minimised by doing an intention-to-treat analysis.

blocks.subtopic: Differential drop-out vs recall bias in treatment trials
blocks.note: Not covered in books/15-1-statistics.pdf as this specific distinction — tested via the question bank: in treatment trials, high differential drop-out (rather than recall bias, which matters more in case-control designs) is the more relevant threat to validity.

blocks.text: Surveillance (detection) bias occurs when disease is better ascertained in a more closely monitored population than in the general population, making an outcome appear more common there without truly occurring more often.

blocks.subtopic: Family (information) aggregation bias — named term
blocks.note: Not covered in books/15-1-statistics.pdf — tested via the question bank: the presence of an affected relative can itself alter how information about a subject is reported or sought, biasing the finding.

blocks.text: Work-up (verification) bias occurs during assessment of a diagnostic test's validity, when execution of the gold-standard reference test is itself influenced by the result of the new instrument being assessed — e.g. the reference test being performed less often when the new test's result is negative.

A hospital-based case-control study is vulnerable to Berkson's bias, Neyman bias, recall bias, and family-information bias — but **NOT** typically to verification/work-up bias, which is specific to diagnostic-test-accuracy studies rather than ordinary case-control designs.

Berkson's (admission-rate) bias results from a difference in the rates of admission of cases and controls, due to the influence of the exposure itself — e.g. in a case-control study of smoking and dementia, the association will tend to be weaker (or even absent) if controls are drawn from a hospital population rather than the community, since smoking causes many diseases that lead to hospitalisation.

Neyman bias (incidence-prevalence bias): when ascertaining causation, one must look for an association between a risk factor and incidence, not prevalence. If a case-control study evaluates a risk factor that kills quickly, it will be under-represented if 'prevalent' rather than 'incident' cases are studied.
Unmasking bias exists when a risk factor unmasks (rather than causes) an event which it is suspected of causing.

blocks.subtopic: "Diagnostic suspicion bias" as a named term
blocks.note: Not covered in books/15-1-statistics.pdf by this name — tested via the question bank: knowledge of a subject's prior exposure to a risk factor can influence the intensity or outcome of a subsequent diagnostic assessment.

source.file: question_bank/Research Methods/EMIs Research Methods_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Observer bias can occur whenever a researcher, knowingly or unknowingly, evaluates a variable depending on the status of the individual under study — e.g. when a research observer knows a subject is on placebo, he may rate them higher on a depression scale. Measurement bias more broadly results from data not being collected in a uniform fashion — e.g. cases interviewed in person while controls are interviewed by telephone; this is minimised by blinding.

blocks.subtopic: Which specific party's blinding guards against cointervention bias
blocks.note: Not covered in books/15-1-statistics.pdf this specifically — tested via the question bank: it is specifically the clinician's blinding (not the assessor's or patient's alone) that guards against cointervention bias, since it is the treating clinician who might otherwise give differential extra care.

blocks.text: Bias direction: 'toward the null' bias yields estimates closer to no-difference; 'away from the null' bias exaggerates the estimate; an extreme case can flip the direction entirely (a true **OR**>1 appearing as <1) — a switch-over bias.

Measurement bias — how variables are recorded
Analysis bias — how drop-outs/crossovers are handled at analysis

Neyman (prevalence-incidence) bias is the risk of assessing outcome long after exposure in a chronic-disease cohort — a 'late look' misses fatal or short-episode cases.

Observer bias in an unblinded depot-vs-oral-antipsychotic trial: an involved, unblinded clinician may differentially probe for symptoms or perceive more improvement depending on the known treatment arm.

bullets.text: Selection bias = study groups differ in factors other than the study variables (sample doesn't represent the target population) — minimised by adequate randomisation.
Response bias = the 'healthy volunteer' effect: responders differ systematically (usually healthier) from non-responders — matters most when evaluating screening tests.
Recall bias: cases/controls recall past exposure differently depending on disease status — case-control studies are particularly vulnerable.
Analysis bias = contamination (participants cross groups) or attrition (lost to follow-up) — minimised by intention-to-treat analysis.

Berkson's bias: hospital-based admission rates for cases/controls differ because of the exposure itself (e.g. smoking causes many hospitalising diseases, weakening a hospital-sourced smoking-dementia association).
Neyman (incidence-prevalence) bias: look for an association with incidence, not prevalence — a risk factor that kills quickly is under-represented among 'prevalent' cases.
Unmasking bias: a risk factor unmasks — rather than causes — the event it's suspected of causing.
Work-up (verification) bias: the gold-standard reference test is performed inconsistently depending on the new test's own result.

Bias direction: 'toward the null' narrows the estimate toward no-difference; 'away from the null' exaggerates it; an extreme case can flip the direction entirely (switch-over bias, e.g. true OR>1 appearing as <1).

blocks.text: Qualitative research explores why people behave as they do, how opinions/attitudes are formed, how people are affected by events around them, how and why cultures develop as they have, and differences between social groups — questions not answerable by quantification alone.

blocks.subtopic: Census as NOT a qualitative method
blocks.note: Not stated explicitly in books/15-1-statistics.pdf — the book's list of 5 qualitative designs (phenomenology, ethnography, grounded theory, case study, participatory action research) does not include census, and separately defines census as a special cross-sectional (quantitative) study — tested via the question bank as an explicit distractor.

blocks.text: Purposeful (purposive) sampling deliberately selects participants relevant to the research question, with no predetermined sample size — data collection continues until theoretical saturation occurs, unlike quantitative research's representative, power-calculated samples.

Theoretical saturation is reached when constant comparison of collected qualitative data generates categories and nothing new is revealed by further comparison — sampling continues until this point, not a predetermined number.

Focus groups are useful for gathering the opinions of service users and providers — conducting interviews in a group format with a predetermined structure to focus discussion, guided by key points (Kitzinger, 1995).

Participatory action research (PAR) involves individuals and groups researching their own personal experiences, socio-cultural settings, and situations — the clear-cut demarcation between researcher and researched found in other research types may not be so apparent here.

Interviews can be structured (a tight schedule of questions, like a questionnaire), semi-structured/'focused' (open-ended questions on pre-selected topic areas, phrasing not dictated by a list), or unstructured/'in-depth' (a limited number of topics in mind, questions framed on the basis of the interviewee's previous response, no fixed order).
Focus groups should usually have 6-10 members; it is not a good idea to run just one group for a whole piece of research — many small groups should be included.

Transcribing (producing a full written script of a recorded interview) is time-consuming — the estimated ratio of time required is about 5:1 (a 10-minute interview needs roughly 50 minutes to transcribe).
Theoretical sampling is the deliberate collection of further, fresh data specifically to test the categories generated so far, distinct from the initial constant-comparison stage.

blocks.subtopic: Qualitative methods NOT appropriate for evaluating treatment response
blocks.note: Not stated as a negative rule in books/15-1-statistics.pdf — the book instead lists qualitative research's appropriate uses (exploring the nature of a problem before planning quantitative research, generating hypotheses, investigating clinical anomalies), implying but not directly stating that outcome/treatment-response evaluation is not one of them.

blocks.text: Reflexivity means sensitivity to the ways the researcher and the research process have shaped the collected data, including the role of the researcher's own prior assumptions and experience, which can influence the results.

Triangulation compares results from two or more methods of data collection or data sources, looking for patterns of convergence to develop or corroborate an overall interpretation. In investigator triangulation specifically, more than one investigator is involved and findings are cross-validated between them.

Ethnography ('portrait of the people') is a methodology for descriptive studies of cultures/peoples sharing something in common (geography, religion, a shared health experience). The emic perspective is an insider's view of their own cultural group; the etic perspective is an outsider's view of the group being studied.

'Reflexivity' (the researcher's awareness of how their own characteristics/preconceptions shaped the data) is commonly confused with 'triangulation' (cross-validating findings across methods, sources, or investigators) — interviewing **BOTH** students and teachers in the same study achieves triangulation, while the interviewer's awareness of her own sex/ethnicity/age effect on responses is reflexivity.

blocks.subtopic: Generalisability as the standard critique of a small qualitative sample's external validity
blocks.note: Not stated explicitly this way in books/15-1-statistics.pdf — tested via the question bank: generalisability (rather than sampling bias or exclusion bias specifically) is the standard concern raised about a small qualitative sample's external validity.

blocks.subtopic: Interviewing multiple stakeholder groups (e.g. students AND teachers)
blocks.note: Not covered in books/15-1-statistics.pdf — tested via the question bank: interviewing more than one stakeholder group in the same qualitative study (e.g. both students and teachers) broadens the range of perspectives captured.

blocks.text: The constant comparative method — central to grounded theory — involves an ongoing comparison of newly collected data against categories already generated, refining and testing those categories as data collection continues, until theoretical saturation is reached.

In qualitative research, purposeful sampling continues — with no predetermined sample size — until theoretical saturation is reached, which is the accepted standard for judging when a qualitative sample is adequate (not a power calculation, as in quantitative research).

blocks.subtopic: Convenience/opportunistic sampling — named term
blocks.note: Not covered in books/15-1-statistics.pdf — tested via the question bank: convenience/opportunistic sampling recruits participants on a first-come-first-served basis rather than through purposeful selection — a weaker, less-favoured qualitative sampling method.

blocks.text: In the **EMI** on qualitative sampling, purposive sampling (deliberately including satisfied, poorly-compliant, early-discontinuing, and persistently-symptomatic users, for breadth) is easily confused with intensity/key-informant sampling (recruiting a small number of topic **EXPERTS**, for depth) — the exam expects you to distinguish breadth-sampling from expertise-sampling.

Psychiatrists = Purposive sampling (deliberately chosen to represent predefined characteristics)
Sample = Snowball sampling (existing participants refer further participants)
Interesting = Intensity/key-informant sampling (a small number of topic experts)
Theories = Theoretical sampling (further data collected specifically to refine an emerging theory)

blocks.title: Named qualitative research designs
rows: Characterising an everyday but poorly defined experience (e.g. 'what is it like to be a carer') — distinct from Jasperian descriptive psychopathology
'Portrait of the people' — emic view = insider perspective of one's own group, etic view = outsider perspective
Glaser & Strauss — constant comparison of data generates categories until theoretical saturation, then theoretical sampling tests them further (e.g. the **DABDA** stages-of-grief model)
A single unit (person/organisation) studied in depth — sits between qualitative and quantitative approaches
Researcher and researched collaborate (e.g. carers co-designing a study on family challenges in schizophrenia)

blocks.text: Beyond interviews and focus groups, observation (field notes, participant vs. non-participant observer) and documents (diaries/letters or formal case notes) are further qualitative data-collection techniques. Analysis-stage distinctions: content analysis splits manifest level (what was literally said) from latent level (what was implied); conversation analysis examines audio/visual, contextual talk; discourse analysis examines personal/autobiographical accounts.

bullets.text: Qualitative research answers 'why/how' questions (behaviour, attitudes, culture, social difference) that quantification alone can't — purposeful sampling continues until theoretical saturation, not a predetermined/power-calculated size.
Interviews: structured (fixed schedule) / semi-structured ('focused', open-ended on set topics) / unstructured ('in-depth', framed off the interviewee's own prior response).
Focus groups: 6-10 members, many small groups rather than one big one — useful for gathering service-user/provider opinions.
Ethnography's emic view = insider's perspective of their own group; etic view = outsider's perspective of the group studied.

Triangulation compares 2+ data sources/methods for convergence; investigator triangulation cross-validates findings between multiple investigators; reflexivity is sensitivity to how the researcher's own assumptions shaped the data.

The constant comparative method (grounded theory) tests and refines categories against new data until theoretical saturation — theoretical sampling is the deliberate further-data-collection step that tests those categories.
Transcribing a recorded interview takes roughly 5x the interview's own length (a 10-min interview needs ~50 min to transcribe).

blocks.text: In secondary research, individual patients are not recruited — eligible studies themselves are 'recruited'.

Narrative reviews are usually written by field experts, broadly aligned with the expert's own opinion and supported by selectively-chosen evidence — generally without a narrow, specific clinical question, and prone to bias since the literature is searched non-methodically ('to suit one's flow of argument'). They cannot be replicated (unless by the same author), but can provide a good introduction to a topic and generate new hypotheses.

The defining feature distinguishing a narrative review from a systematic review is its search method: narrative reviews are 'searched in a random manner to suit one's flow of argument,' not methodically — whereas a systematic review follows rigorous, reproducible steps to identify relevant literature, appraise individual studies, and synthesise a conclusion.
RCTs are the most frequently combined study design in a meta-analysis, though it is possible to combine other study designs too.

Meta-analysis/systematic-review quality depends on: a comprehensive literature search, clearly defined eligibility criteria, a clearly defined and strictly adhered-to protocol, and predetermined criteria for trial quality. If primary studies are poor quality, even sound statistical procedures produce a meaningless result — the GIGO ('garbage in, garbage out') principle.

Weighting of individual studies within a meta-analysis is based on sample size, precision, external validity (generalisability), and methodological quality — assigned independently of the study's own outcome.

blocks.subtopic: Analysing methodologically-divergent primary studies as two separate meta-analyses
blocks.note: Not covered in books/15-1-statistics.pdf — tested via the question bank: when primary studies differ substantially in methodology, the correct approach is to analyse the two sets of studies as two independent meta-analyses, rather than forcing them into a single pooled fixed- or random-effects estimate.

blocks.text: The most common method to detect publication bias is to check for asymmetry in an (inverted) funnel plot — small studies are more likely to remain unpublished if their results are non-significant, producing asymmetry. Visual inspection of funnel plots is often unreliable, so several statistical tests exist to quantify the asymmetry.

For continuous outcomes, the standardised difference between means (**SMD**) — dividing the raw mean difference by the pooled standard deviation of the two groups — is scale-free, which is what makes pooling data from studies using different measurement instruments possible. Cohen's d and Hedges' g are two formulas for calculating it, Hedges' g avoiding a bias seen in Cohen's d with small numbers of subjects.

Identifying grey literature — unpublished conference abstracts, presentations, and posters — is one of the required elements of a proper literature search, alongside using multiple databases, cross-checking reference lists, hand-searching, and approaching experts about missing studies.

blocks.subtopic: Publication bias driven mainly by non-submission, not editorial rejection (Dickersin et al.)
blocks.note: Not covered in books/15-1-statistics.pdf this specifically (the book defines publication bias generally as authors submitting and/or editors publishing mainly significant results, without attributing the dominant cause) — tested via the question bank: publication bias is driven mainly by researchers failing to submit null/unimportant findings for publication (the 'file drawer problem'), rather than by editors/reviewers rejecting submitted manuscripts (Dickersin, Min & Meinert, JAMA 1992).

blocks.subtopic: Why meta-analyses are needed (low power of individual studies vs GIGO)
blocks.note: Not covered in books/15-1-statistics.pdf this specifically — the book warns that pooling cannot fix poor-quality primary studies (GIGO, see above), but does not explicitly state that meta-analyses are needed chiefly because individual primary studies often lack sufficient statistical power on their own.

blocks.subtopic: Gene Glass coining the term 'meta-analysis' (1976)
blocks.note: Not covered in books/15-1-statistics.pdf — tested via the question bank: Gene Glass coined the term 'meta-analysis' in 1976, describing it as the 'analysis of analyses'.

items.text: A meta-analysis study's weighting depends on sample size, precision, external validity and methodological rigour — **NEVER** on the direction or magnitude of its reported outcome, which is a commonly offered but incorrect distractor.

Publication bias is driven mainly by authors failing to **SUBMIT** null/unimportant findings (the 'file drawer problem'), not primarily by editors rejecting submitted manuscripts — a common misconception this question bank targets directly.

When primary studies differ in underlying **METHODOLOGY** (not just in numeric spread) — e.g. some dichotomising an exposure while others treat it continuously — the correct response is to run two **SEPARATE** meta-analyses, not to force everything into one pooled fixed- or random-effects estimate.

blocks.text: A comprehensive literature search uses multiple databases (not MEDLINE/CINAHL alone), cross-checks reference lists, hand-searches, consults experts, and identifies grey literature (conference abstracts/posters). Individual-patient-data meta-analysis (contacting original authors for raw data) is more powerful than summary-data meta-analysis but far less often achievable.

Heterogeneity has 3 flavours: clinical (different but theoretically combinable interventions/populations — describable, not measurable), methodological (different study methods), and statistical (inconsistent quantitative results — testable via chi-square/Cochran's Q or I²). Rule of thumb: an average chi-square equals its degrees of freedom (n−1 studies); these tests have low power, so a non-significant result does **NOT** prove homogeneity.

Each study has its own true effect, normally distributed around a mean
Valid only if significant heterogeneity can be excluded
Gives smaller studies proportionally more weight

blocks.title: Meta-analysis statistical model ↔ method pairing
rows: Mantel-Haenszel (**OR**, rate/risk ratios) or Peto (approximates **OR**) — neither adjusts for confounding

blocks.text: Publication bias (significant/'positive' results are more likely published) produces an asymmetric funnel plot (effect size on x-axis, precision/sample size or 1/SE on y-axis). Failsafe N (Rosenthal & Cooper) estimates how many null-effect 'file drawer' studies would be needed to nullify an observed effect; the trim-and-fill procedure (Duval & Tweedie, 2000) imputes missing studies and recomputes the effect as a sensitivity check; cumulative meta-analysis (adding studies from largest/most precise to smallest) shows whether the pooled estimate shifts as smaller studies are added — a shift signals bias.

Effect-size measures: for dichotomous outcomes, **OR**/**RR** are preferred (less dependent on baseline risk than absolute risk); **OR** overestimates **RR** increasingly as event rates rise above ~==20%==, so **RR** is preferred in Cochrane reviews when events are common. For continuous outcomes: simple mean difference (**DM**) or standardised mean difference (**SMD** = DM / pooled SD), calculated as Cohen's d or Hedges' g (the latter corrects Cohen's d's small-sample bias).

Forest plot ('blobbogram') construction: each study is a blob/square (point estimate) sized by weight, with a horizontal line for its 95% CI; the pooled result is a diamond lozenge with minimal width (highest precision); a vertical 'line of no effect' sits at 1 for ratio measures (OR/RR) or 0 for mean-difference/SMD measures — a study whose CI line crosses the line of no effect is not statistically significant even if heavily weighted.

blocks.subtopic: Worked forest-plot NNT/ARR/relative-benefit example (antidepressant relapse prevention)
blocks.note: Not covered in books/15-1-statistics.pdf as this specific worked numeric example — tested via the question bank: reading a forest plot, the pooled experimental/control event rates can be read directly off the plot; NNT is the reciprocal of the absolute risk reduction (ARR); relative benefit/risk reduction is (CER-EER)/CER. A worked antidepressant relapse-prevention meta-analysis gave a pooled EER of 0.18, an MAOI-specific CER of 0.86, an overall NNT of approximately 4, and an SSRI-specific relative benefit of approximately 0.58.

bullets.text: In secondary research, eligible studies themselves are 'recruited' — not individual patients.

Narrative reviews reflect an expert's own opinion, are searched non-methodically, and cannot be replicated — but can introduce a topic and generate hypotheses. Systematic reviews use a focused question, comprehensive/uniform search and selection, and (optionally) quantitative synthesis.

Meta-analysis/systematic-review quality depends on a comprehensive search, clear eligibility criteria, a strictly-followed protocol, and predetermined trial-quality criteria — poor primary studies still produce a meaningless result (GIGO) even with sound pooling statistics.
Study weighting in a meta-analysis is based on sample size, precision, external validity, and methodological quality — assigned independently of the study's own outcome.

Fixed-effects: one common true effect across studies, valid only once heterogeneity is excluded, narrower CIs. Random-effects: each study's own true effect varies around a mean, used when heterogeneity is present, gives smaller studies more weight, wider/less precise CIs.

Heterogeneity has 3 flavours: clinical (describable, not measurable), methodological (describable, not measurable), and statistical (testable via chi-square/Cochran's Q or I²). Low test power means a non-significant result does **NOT** prove homogeneity.

Funnel-plot asymmetry is the classic sign of publication bias (small non-significant studies go unpublished) — visual inspection is unreliable, so formal statistical tests are used to confirm true asymmetry.

For dichotomous outcomes, OR/RR are preferred over absolute risk; OR increasingly overestimates RR above ~20% event rates, so RR is preferred in Cochrane reviews for common events. For continuous outcomes, SMD (Cohen's d or Hedges' g) is scale-free, enabling cross-study pooling.

A proper literature search uses multiple databases, cross-checks reference lists, hand-searches, approaches experts, and identifies grey literature (unpublished conference abstracts, presentations, posters).

blocks.subtopic: QALY as an explicit life-years × utility-weight formula
blocks.note: Not stated as an explicit formula in books/15-1-statistics.pdf — the book discusses QALYs as the output measure of cost-utility analysis (see below) without spelling out the life-years x utility-weight calculation itself.

blocks.text: Cost-minimisation analysis is used when both/all interventions produce the SAME outcome — hence only the costs are compared (e.g. Clozaril vs Zaponex, two brands of clozapine, at £3.50 vs £3.11 per tablet).

Cost-utility analysis is used when, beyond the clinical effect, one must also holistically consider disease burden, side effects, and social impact — output is measured in life-utility units such as QALYs or DALYs (e.g. £12,500 spent per QALY gained with Clozaril vs £10,500 per QALY with Zaponex).

Cost-benefit analysis is used when two interventions with different clinical outcomes are compared by translating ALL outcomes into monetary terms — e.g. deciding between running a clozapine clinic or opening a service-user forum. This is often used by managers deciding how to spend allocated money.

blocks.text: Direct costs: hospital space, drugs, equipment, and salaries of doctors and other professionals. Indirect costs: loss of productivity for the patient, cost of a caretaker for a dependant (child/pet) while the patient is hospitalised. Intangible (unmeasurable) costs: pain and suffering, social stigma, physical discomfort. Opportunity cost: the value of the opportunity lost by choosing one option over another (every action carries one).

Health-state preference measures: a visual-analogue rating scale (0 = death, max = perfect health); time trade-off (how many remaining life-years would be spent to be cured); standard gamble (what odds of death vs cure would someone accept from a risky curative intervention); and willingness-to-pay (WTP) — how much someone would pay to prevent or cure a health state.

Incremental Cost-Effectiveness Ratio (**ICER**) = [cost of proposed intervention − cost of control] / [effect of proposed intervention − effect of control] — the additional cost per unit of additional health gained. Simply subtracting cost-per-patient-recovered between two interventions (rather than calculating the true incremental ratio) is a common and misleading shortcut.

Sensitivity-analysis subtypes for economic evaluations: one-way analysis (changing one variable, which can underestimate uncertainty); extreme-scenario analysis (setting a variable to its max/min, which overestimates uncertainty); two-way analysis (varying two variables together — unwieldy for more, hence Monte Carlo simulation for 3+ variables); Monte-Carlo simulation (assumes a probability distribution for each uncertain input); and bootstrapping (resampling the original dataset rather than varying observed parameters).
Opportunity cost is the cost of a wasted opportunity — e.g. the cost of missing a business meeting because one attended a dental appointment instead. Every action carries an opportunity cost.

A Cost-Effectiveness Acceptability Curve (**CEAC**) indicates the probability that an intervention is cost-effective compared to the alternative, given the observed data, across a range of λ (willingness-to-pay) values — a way of summarising the uncertainty in cost-effectiveness estimates.

rows: Not clinically effective — needs further study

blocks.text: Standard gamble: imagine a risky intervention for a health state that either cures (if it succeeds) or kills (if it fails) — respondents are asked what odds of success vs death they would accept to be cured, and their preferred value is recorded.

blocks.subtopic: Implicit costs — named term
blocks.note: Not covered in books/15-1-statistics.pdf — the book's own cost taxonomy is direct/indirect/intangible/opportunity costs (see above), with no separate 'implicit costs' category — tested via the question bank: implicit costs describe the benefits foregone by a particular use of health resources, often estimated via the indirect costs of the next-best alternative use of the same resources.

blocks.text: Worked incremental-value example: comparing CBT (£1000/course, 5/10 recover) against Graded Exercise Therapy (£900/course, 4/10 recover) for Chronic Fatigue Syndrome. It is tempting but wrong to conclude the extra £100 buys one extra recovery (£2250−£2000=£250). The correct incremental calculation: £10,000 for 5 recoveries via CBT vs £9,000 for 4 recoveries via GET means an extra £1,000 is spent for each additional recovery — this incremental calculation (the basis of ICER) must always be done when comparing two interventions economically.

The 'viewpoint' from which an economic analysis calculates costs and benefits materially changes its conclusions — government/health-ministry, service-user, public-health-body (e.g. WHO), and clinician viewpoints can each differ, so a study's conclusions must be interpreted in the context of the viewpoint(s) it employed.

blocks.subtopic: Non-RCT clinical-effectiveness data as a methodological weakness in economic analysis
blocks.note: Not covered in books/15-1-statistics.pdf — tested via the question bank: deriving the clinical-effectiveness data used in an economic analysis from a non-randomised sample (rather than an RCT) is a recognised methodological weakness, even when the cost data themselves are well collected — an economic analysis inherits the rigour of its effectiveness data source.

items.text: Time trade-off is a health-state **PREFERENCE**/utility-elicitation technique, not a sensitivity-analysis method — don't confuse it with the tested sensitivity-analysis subtypes (one-way, worst-case, Monte Carlo, bootstrapping).

A Cost-Effectiveness Acceptability Curve (**CEAC**) tells you only the relative **PROBABILITY** that each option is cost-effective at a given willingness-to-pay — it can never itself identify which intervention is the most clinically effective.

The 'viewpoint' from which an economic analysis calculates its costs changes the conclusion: counting only bed-days/hospitalisation costs reflects the **SERVICE-PROVIDER**'s viewpoint specifically — not society's, the patient's, or carers'.

blocks.text: Nixon's permutation matrix pools multiple economic evaluations without a formal meta-analysis: incremental cost and incremental effect pairs from each study are cross-tabulated onto a single cost-effectiveness plane so results can be compared visually across studies.

**ACER** (average cost-effectiveness ratio) = cost/effect for a single intervention on its own — distinct from **ICER**, which compares the incremental cost and effect of one intervention against a specific comparator.

bullets.text: Cost-minimisation assumes equal outcomes, comparing costs alone. Cost-utility uses QALY/DALY output. Cost-benefit converts ALL outcomes to money. Cost-effectiveness uses a natural clinical-scale outcome. Cost-consequences lists costs/outcomes disaggregated, not combined.

Direct costs (hospital/drugs/staff), indirect costs (productivity loss, caretaker costs), intangible costs (pain/stigma), and opportunity cost (value of the next-best foregone option) are the 4 cost dimensions.

ICER = (cost of proposed − cost of control) / (effect of proposed − effect of control) — the extra cost per unit of extra health gained. Simple cost-per-recovery subtraction between two arms is a common wrong shortcut.
5 sensitivity-analysis subtypes: one-way, extreme-scenario (over-estimates uncertainty), two-way, Monte-Carlo (3+ variables), bootstrapping (resamples the dataset).

Cost-effectiveness plane: SE = intervention preferred (lower cost, better effect); NW = reject (higher cost, worse effect); NE = needs judgement (higher cost, better effect); SW = not clinically effective (lower cost, worse effect).
The 'viewpoint' taken (government, service-user, WHO, clinician) materially changes an economic analysis's conclusions — always interpret ICER/cost figures in the context of whose viewpoint was used.

sections.title: 10. Quality Improvement (a separate SPMM chapter, kept here for this app's topic grouping)

blocks.subtopic: Quality Improvement (QI) — definition
blocks.note: No book PDF covers Quality Improvement in this corpus (the manifest assigns only books/15-1-statistics.pdf to research-methods, which is Study Designs/Bias/Causality/etc. — QI is a separate SPMM curriculum chapter with no book source here) — tested via the question bank: Quality Improvement (**QI**) is a scientific approach that combines systematic analysis of current performance with interventions to improve it, aimed at ensuring the quality and safety of health service provision.

blocks.subtopic: QI vs research — logical structure and scope of intervention
blocks.note: No book PDF covers Quality Improvement in this corpus (the manifest assigns only books/15-1-statistics.pdf to research-methods, which is Study Designs/Bias/Causality/etc. — QI is a separate SPMM curriculum chapter with no book source here) — tested via the question bank: **QI** projects share much of the logical structure of research (a prediction/hypothesis, a measured test of change, assessment of impact) but the interventions they test remain **WITHIN** established standards of care — i.e. **QI** interventions are not novel, unlike research interventions.

blocks.subtopic: PDSA (Plan-Do-Study-Act) cycles
blocks.note: No book PDF covers Quality Improvement in this corpus (the manifest assigns only books/15-1-statistics.pdf to research-methods, which is Study Designs/Bias/Causality/etc. — QI is a separate SPMM curriculum chapter with no book source here) — tested via the question bank: **PDSA** (Plan-Do-Study-Act) cycles structure the iterative testing of a change, integrating top-down ideas with bottom-up observation before wider implementation — the method originates from Shewhart and Deming's industrial quality-improvement work.

blocks.subtopic: Root Cause Analysis (RCA)
blocks.note: No book PDF covers Quality Improvement in this corpus (the manifest assigns only books/15-1-statistics.pdf to research-methods, which is Study Designs/Bias/Causality/etc. — QI is a separate SPMM curriculum chapter with no book source here) — tested via the question bank: Root Cause Analysis (**RCA**) is a retrospective-only **QI** method, triggered after a sentinel/adverse event (e.g. an inpatient suicide) to identify putative causal factors — but it is event-specific and prone to hindsight bias, so its findings may not generalise to the system as a whole.

blocks.subtopic: Pareto chart
blocks.note: No book PDF covers Quality Improvement in this corpus (the manifest assigns only books/15-1-statistics.pdf to research-methods, which is Study Designs/Bias/Causality/etc. — QI is a separate SPMM curriculum chapter with no book source here) — tested via the question bank: A Pareto chart re-orders a bar chart from most- to least-frequent category (sometimes with a superimposed cumulative-frequency line), applying the 80/20 rule to visually identify the small number of high-yield causes responsible for most of the problems.

blocks.subtopic: QI's systems focus (vs individual blame)
blocks.note: No book PDF covers Quality Improvement in this corpus (the manifest assigns only books/15-1-statistics.pdf to research-methods, which is Study Designs/Bias/Causality/etc. — QI is a separate SPMM curriculum chapter with no book source here) — tested via the question bank: Genuine **QI** activity focuses on systems (e.g. evaluating whether a team's culture encourages clinicians to report errors), avoiding blame attribution — this is distinct from investigations aimed at identifying which individual staff member was at fault after an adverse event.

blocks.subtopic: PDCA (Plan-Do-Check-Act) vs PDSA
blocks.note: No book PDF covers Quality Improvement in this corpus (the manifest assigns only books/15-1-statistics.pdf to research-methods, which is Study Designs/Bias/Causality/etc. — QI is a separate SPMM curriculum chapter with no book source here) — tested via the question bank: **PDCA** (Plan-Do-Check-Act) is sometimes used interchangeably with **PDSA**, but is better reserved for error-correction/fault-detection contexts rather than quality improvement proper.

blocks.subtopic: Lean Thinking
blocks.note: No book PDF covers Quality Improvement in this corpus (the manifest assigns only books/15-1-statistics.pdf to research-methods, which is Study Designs/Bias/Causality/etc. — QI is a separate SPMM curriculum chapter with no book source here) — tested via the question bank: Lean Thinking is a management philosophy centred on reducing waste and resource consumption while preserving value and improving overall user satisfaction — distinct from **PDSA**, **FADE**, or Failure Mode and Effects Analysis.

blocks.subtopic: SQUIRE reporting checklist
blocks.note: No book PDF covers Quality Improvement in this corpus (the manifest assigns only books/15-1-statistics.pdf to research-methods, which is Study Designs/Bias/Causality/etc. — QI is a separate SPMM curriculum chapter with no book source here) — tested via the question bank: **SQUIRE** (Standards for Quality Improvement Reporting Excellence) is the consensus 19-item checklist recommended for reporting formal healthcare **QI** studies (Ogrinc et al., 2008) — distinct from **PRISMA**, **STARD**, or **MOOSE** checklists used for other study types.

blocks.subtopic: Worked QI project example (tamoxifen/fluoxetine co-prescribing)
blocks.note: No book PDF covers Quality Improvement in this corpus (the manifest assigns only books/15-1-statistics.pdf to research-methods, which is Study Designs/Bias/Causality/etc. — QI is a separate SPMM curriculum chapter with no book source here) — tested via the question bank: A real-world **QI** project example: searching **GP** registries for patients co-prescribed tamoxifen and **fluoxetine** (a known interacting pair), contacting affected patients, presenting the evidence to GPs, and building a computer alert to flag future co-prescribing — this combination of measurement plus a systematic change is what defines a **QI** (not case-series, cohort, or case-control) study.

blocks.subtopic: Statistical formulas & significance testing
blocks.note: This question bank barely touches core inferential statistics (p-values, confidence intervals, standard error, sample-size/power-calculation mechanics) beyond passing mentions (e.g., that response rate is not the same as power). Core Paper B statistics content is covered separately under this repo's 'statistics' topic — do not rely on this research-methods guide for statistical formulas or hypothesis-testing mechanics.

blocks.subtopic: Diagnostic test accuracy (sensitivity, specificity, ROC, likelihood ratios)
blocks.note: Verification (work-up) bias is defined only once, in passing, as the answer explaining why it does **NOT** apply to ordinary case-control studies. Sensitivity, specificity, positive/negative predictive value, **ROC** curves, and likelihood ratios are not covered anywhere in this question bank — check the statistics or evidence-based-medicine topic notes in this repo for that content.
